findings.content: The real `react-native-haptic-feedback` package exposes a default export whose `trigger` accepts (type, options) and also exposes extra helpers (e.g. `Haptics`/`impact`/`selection`). This mock only stubs a bare `trigger`, and does not mirror the default-export shape. If callers import the module via `import ReactNativeHapticFeedback from ...` and call additional methods (or destructure them), tests will fail at runtime with `undefined is not a function`. Since no callers exist in the repo yet, at minimum mirror the real module's shape (expose `trigger` accepting a type+options, and a default export) to keep the mock robust.

These broad patterns exclude ALL `.ts/.tsx/.js/.jsx/.json/.md/.yml/.yaml` files (recursively) from the Docker build context. This removes essential files such as `package.json`, `app.json` (confirmed to exist in this repo), `tsconfig.json`, `babel.config.js`, and `metro.config.js`, which are required for `npm install` and the Expo/Metro build. The Docker build will effectively receive an empty/non-buildable context. Replace these wildcards with specific, targeted ignores (e.g. only ignore root-level `*.map` files or exclude specific non-essential files), and re-allow critical config files with a negated pattern (e.g. `!package.json`, `!app.json`, `!tsconfig.json`, `!babel.config.js`).

Ignoring `app.config.js`/`app.config.json` excludes the Expo app configuration from the build context. Expo requires the app config to resolve the project name/slug, plugins, and bundle identifiers; without it the Docker image will fail to build or produce an incorrectly configured app. These files should not be excluded from the build context.

Excluding `package-lock.json`, `yarn.lock`, and `pnpm-lock.yaml` from the build context undermines dependency reproducibility. Inside the container the package manager will resolve dependency versions on its own (often a fixed/newer version than the lockfile), leading to inconsistent, non-reproducible images and potential builds that behave differently than local development. Lock files should be kept in the build context.

Redundant ignore entries hurt maintainability and invite drift: `dist/` is listed here in the build outputs section and again under the Expo section, and `*.log` / `dist/` appear multiple times elsewhere in the file. If one copy is edited (e.g. turned into an allow pattern) and the other is not, behavior becomes inconsistent. Consolidate these duplicate patterns into a single canonical location.

Ignoring `app.config.js` and `app.config.json` means ESLint won't lint these Expo configuration sources, which often contain runtime logic (plugins, env handling, conditional config helpers). JS-based Expo configs are widely linted in practice. Consider removing these from the ignore list (or at least only ignoring `app.config.json`) so config regressions are caught by lint, and keep the equivalent entries in `.gitignore`/`.easignore` instead of here.
`*.log` is already listed near the top of the file and `logs/` is ignored there too; the duplicate `*.log` under the "Expo development" section is redundant and can be dropped to keep the file clean.

Duplicate pattern: `dist/` is defined both here and in the Build outputs section (line 9). Duplicate rules are redundant and can cause maintenance inconsistencies when one is updated and the other is not. Remove the duplicate in one section and keep a single canonical rule.

Duplicate pattern: `web-build/` is defined both here (Expo section) and again in the Expo web section at the bottom of the file. Keeping two identical rules risks them drifting out of sync. Consolidate into a single entry.

Inconsistent package-lock handling: `yarn.lock` and `pnpm-lock.yaml` are ignored here, but `package-lock.json` is not. Lock files are generated artifacts that should generally not be committed (or, conversely, all handled consistently according to project policy). Ignoring only some package managers' lock files creates non-reproducible and inconsistent builds depending on which package manager a contributor uses. Add `package-lock.json` here (and `npm-shrinkwrap.json` if used) for consistency.

findings.content: Excluding all `*.d.ts` files will strip TypeScript type declarations from the published npm package. If this package ships compiled `.js` outputs alongside type definitions (e.g. declarations generated into the root), downstream TypeScript consumers lose the typed API and fall back to `any`. Unless the package intentionally does not provide types (e.g. it's an application rather than a library), this rule should be removed or restricted so declarations inside the publish root are not filtered out.

Ignoring `*.min.js` and `*.min.map` may accidentally exclude pre-minified production bundles that the package is meant to distribute. If the published entrypoint or shipped assets include minified files at the package root (common for libraries that publish a minified browser bundle), this rule will silently drop them and break the published artifact. Verify whether any minified distribution files are expected to be published; if so, scope the exemption accordingly.

The `*.map` rule excludes all source maps. If the package ships generated `.map` files for debugging its shipped bundles, this rule removes them entirely, degrading debuggability of published code. Confirm that dropping all source maps at the package root is intentional.

Excluding `app.config.js` / `app.config.json` from the published package could break runtime config resolution if consumers rely on Expo config in the installed package. For most published libraries this config is not required, but if the package is intended to be consumed as an Expo project dependency and reads these files at runtime, absence of the config may cause failures. Confirm this exclusion is intentional for the publish scenario.

The pattern `*.log` is already listed at line 11 under '# Logs'. This duplicate under '# Expo development' is redundant and can cause maintenance inconsistencies (e.g., if one location is updated but not the other). Remove this duplicate occurrence.

`package-lock.json`, `yarn.lock`, and `pnpm-lock.yaml` are already listed in the '# Package manager lock files' section (lines 57-59). This entire '# Lock files' block is a redundant duplicate that adds no value and risks drift between the two copies. Remove these duplicate entries.

The `@/hooks` alias maps to `./src/hooks`, but no `src/hooks` directory exists in this project and no source file imports from `@/hooks`. This alias is dead/misleading configuration — any future import using it will silently fail at resolution time. Either create the directory if hooks are planned, or remove this alias entry to avoid a resolution trap.

Requiring a `.ts` file with `require()` will fail at runtime in standard Node.js unless a TypeScript loader/compiler hook (e.g. ts-node, esbuild-register) is registered. This debug script will crash with `ERR_UNKNOWN_FILE_EXTENSION` (or Module._extensions['.ts'] error) before any test runs. Compile the dependency to JS or use a loader before running.

`error.message` assumes the caught value is always an Error instance. If `ChecklistSchema.parse` ever throws a non-Error value (e.g. a string, or a ZodError where message may not be the only detail), accessing `.message` on `undefined`/non-object will itself throw a TypeError and crash the script mid-report. Use a safe accessor such as `error instanceof Error ? error.message : String(error)` in the catch block.

Device specs and app build paths are hardcoded (e.g., 'iPhone 14' / 'iOS 16.4', the Debug app path under ios/build). The pre-commit/commit-msg hook references `commitlint`, and the `config.commitizen` block references `cz-conventional-changelog`/`commitizen`, but neither of these tools is declared in `devDependencies`. Add `@commitlint/cli`, `@commitlint/config-conventional`, `commitizen`, and `cz-conventional-changelog` to `devDependencies` (and a commitlint config) so the hooks work after `npm install`.

The `config.commitizen` references the `cz-conventional-changelog` adapter, but the `commitizen` CLI and `cz-conventional-changelog` package are not listed in `devDependencies`. `@react-native/babel-preset` is pinned to `^0.87.1` while the runtime is `react-native 0.86.3` (and the tested preset version is the jest preset `@react-native/jest-preset ^0.86.3`). findings.content: OSTYPE detection is unreliable. On Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL), OSTYPE is typically 'linux', and in Git Bash/MSYS it is 'msys', but on native Windows cmd/PowerShell invoking the script OSTYPE is often empty. So the check will falsely reject WSL (where the script is exactly intended to run) and may also wrongfully accept other platforms. Use multiple OS detection signals, e.g. also check for MSYSTEM, or /proc/version on WSL, or fall back to 'uname', and avoid blocking WSL.

The Python check is not portable across Windows setups. On many Windows installs the interpreter is launched via `py` or `python3` rather than `python`, and on minimal systems `python` may not be on PATH while `python3` exists (which would be available in WSL). Also `python --version` on some versions writes to stderr, so the captured PYTHON_VERSION may be empty. Consider checking `python`/`python3`/`py` in order and capturing stderr (e.g. `python --version 2>&1`).

The exit-code check is incorrect: `$?` is evaluated only after `npm run typecheck`, so a failing `npm run lint` is silently ignored (its exit status is overwritten). Capture each command's exit status separately, e.g. `npm run lint; LINT=$?; npm run typecheck; TYPECHECK=$?` and fail/warn if either is non-zero. Also `if [ $? -ne 0 ]` should not be used after a compound sequence for this reason.

Since `useState` only reads the initializer on mount, this recomputation is wasted work on every render. Use lazy state initializers or `useMemo` to compute it only when needed.

State is initialized from `initialDate` only once on mount. Because the `Modal` stays mounted (visibility is controlled via the `visible` prop, not conditional rendering), every time the sheet is reopened the calendar still shows the previous `viewYear`/`viewMonth` and previously selected day — even if `initialDate` changed. This makes the picker display stale data. Add a `useEffect` that resets `viewYear`/`viewMonth`/`selected` from `initialDate` whenever `visible` becomes true (or the initial date changes).

Accessibility concern: the color swatch exposes raw hex codes (e.g. '#FF6B6B') as the accessibility label, which is not meaningful to screen-reader users. Consider mapping each option to a human-readable color name (e.g. '#FF6B6B' -> 'Coral Red') and using that in both `accessibilityLabel` and `accessibilityHint`.

HapticFeedback.light() fires unconditionally on every submit, then HapticFeedback.error() is triggered separately on validation failure, which can produce a conflicting double-haptic (light followed by error). Simplify so haptics reflect the outcome: emit only the success/light haptic inside the validation-success branch and the error haptic in the failure branch, rather than always emitting light first.

The navigation object is cast to an ad-hoc `{ navigate: (route: string) => void }` type, which bypasses the project's static navigation type checks. If the 'Teams' route name ever changes or is not registered under the current navigator, this fails silently at runtime. Prefer using a typed navigation helper (e.g., `CompositeNavigationProp` or the typed route param list) so route names are validated at compile time.

`renderTeam` is defined inline inside the component, so a new function reference is created on every render. Combined with the inline `renderItem={renderTeam}`, this defeats FlatList's row memoization for large team lists. Consider memoizing the renderer with `useCallback` (or extracting it out of the component) to avoid unnecessary re-renders.

Both the backdrop (`team-picker-backdrop`) and the header ✕ close button expose the identical accessibility label 'Close team selector'. This can confuse screen-reader users because two seemingly different elements do the same thing. Give them distinct roles/labels (e.g., the backdrop could be an accessibility view that dismisses, or the ✕ button should have its own label like 'Dismiss selector') so the semantics are clear.

State is only initialized once from `initialTime` via `useState`, but the `Modal` stays mounted and is shown/hidden through the `visible` prop. Because of this, the picker is never reset: if `initialTime` changes between opens (or the user closes without confirming and reopens), the sheet will show the stale previously-selected values instead of the new `initialTime`. The recomputed `initial`/`initial12` on each render have no effect after the first mount. Reset the state when the sheet (re)opens — e.g. with a `useEffect` keyed on `visible`/`initialTime` (when `visible` becomes true) that sets `hour12`, `minute`, and `period` from the fresh `initialTime`.

The bottom tab navigator is created without a type parameter (`createBottomTabNavigator()`), even though a dedicated `MainTabParamList` type already exists in `src/types/index.ts` (routes Main/Teams/Safety/Settings). Without it, tab route names are untyped `string`s, so a typo in a route name silently falls through to the `ellipse` fallback icon at runtime instead of being caught at compile time. Type it for consistency with the stack navigator: `createBottomTabNavigator<MainTabParamList>()` (and import that type).
findings.suggestion_code: const Tab = createBottomTabNavigator<MainTabParamList>();

findings.content: This `else` branch assigning the fallback `'ellipse'` icon is effectively dead code: all four tab routes (Main, Teams, Safety, Settings) are known and handled above. Its presence masks typos/mismatches in route names (e.g. `'Teams'` written as `'Teems'`) by silently rendering a placeholder glyph rather than surfacing the error. Prefer removing the fallback or using a type-safe route lookup so unknown names fail loudly.

`headerBackTitleVisible` is deprecated in current React Navigation (v6+) and will be removed, being superseded by `headerBackButtonDisplayMode: 'minimal'`. This can also produce deprecated-option warnings on iOS. Consider migrating to `headerBackButtonDisplayMode` to keep the codebase up to date.

findings.content: In-place sort is called directly on `state.data.data.practices` inside the memo callback. Because `.sort()` mutates the source array, the original array becomes permanently reordered on every render, which can corrupt the source of truth in context/state and produce inconsistent UI if other consumers rely on the original ordering. Copy before sorting: `return [...practices].sort(...)`.

The empty-state text uses a nested ternary, which violates the readability rule. Additionally, since `ListEmptyComponent` only renders when the list is empty, `filteredPractices.length === 0` is always truthy here, so the outer else branch (`'No practices found'`) and the outer condition are effectively dead. Simplify to a single ternary based on `selectedTeam`.

A practice can legitimately have zero checklist entries (the UI shows an empty-state message for this case), so exporting it will throw inside the try/catch and show only a generic 'Failed to export data'. Guard against the empty-array case before computing max/average heat index.

findings.content: The saving indicator is reset on a 0ms timer in the same handler, so `savingNotes` flips back to `false` almost immediately after being set to `true`. The disabled/opacity style tied to `savingNotes` provides no meaningful visual feedback. Either remove the saving state entirely (the dispatch is synchronous) or keep it `true` until the persistence actually completes.

The pull-to-refresh spinner never appears: `refreshing` is never set to `true`, so the `RefreshControl` is always false and this handler is effectively a no-op. Remove the dead `refreshing` state / `RefreshControl` wiring, or actually drive the spinner (e.g., set `setRefreshing(true)` then `false` after the refresh resolves) if real refresh behavior is intended.

`deletingChecklist` is only ever written (via `setDeletingChecklist`) and never read, so it triggers unnecessary re-renders on every delete without providing any UI feedback. The value is ignored in the destructure. Either remove this dead state entirely or use it to drive a loading/disabled indicator on the deleted row.

Debug `console.log` statements (practiceId mounted, add/edit/delete actions) appear to have been left in production code. Consider removing them or gating them behind a logger/debug flag to avoid leaking state and noisy logs in production.

findings.content: The app version 'Version 1.0.0' is hardcoded directly in the JSX. This will drift out of sync whenever the version changes. It should be sourced from a central app config (e.g., expo-constants or a shared constants file) so the displayed version always matches the actual build version.

The `footer` and `footerText` style definitions are declared but never referenced anywhere in the component (no `<View style={styles.footer}>` or `<Text style={styles.footerText}>` exist in the JSX). This is dead code and should be removed to keep the style sheet clean.

ID generation via `Date.now()` can produce duplicate IDs when two teams are created within the same millisecond (or when the clock is adjusted). Duplicate ids break `FlatList` `keyExtractor` uniqueness and can cause two records to collide in the reducer/list state, leading to silent data loss or React key warnings. Use a collision-resistant generator (e.g., `crypto.randomUUID()`/`expo-crypto`, or a monotonically incremented counter/`useRef`) instead.

findings.content: `handleSubmitTeam` unconditionally closes the modal after calling `dispatch`, but there is no error handling if the reducer rejects or the update fails (e.g., duplicate name or reducer business-rule failure). In such a case the user gets no feedback and their input is silently lost. Wrap the dispatch in a try/catch and surface an Alert on failure (or keep the modal open) so failures are visible to the user.

The swipe-to-delete row (`SwipeableRow`) does not provide any accessibility affordance for the delete action in this screen. Screen-reader users have no reachable way to delete a team, since the visible card only opens the editor on press. Ensure `SwipeableRow` exposes an accessible delete action (e.g., an accessible button/label announced by screen readers) and wire `onDelete`/`deleteLabel` through to it.

**Race condition on initial mount overwrites persisted data with seed data.** On first render `state.loading` is `false` and `state.error` is `null`, so this save effect fires immediately, writing the hardcoded `initialState.data` (the mock seed) to AsyncStorage before the load effect's `AsyncStorage.getItem` completes. The two effects capture the same render where `loading === false`, so the seed `setItem` races with / overwrites the real stored data. Guard saving until the initial load has finished — e.g. track an explicit `hydrated` flag (set only after load resolves) and require `hydrated` before calling `saveData()`. Relying solely on `state.loading` is insufficient because it is false both before load starts and after it completes.

**Top-level `version`/`lastSync` become stale on every mutation.** ADD/UPDATE/DELETE for teams, practices, and checklists (e.g. this ADD_TEAM case and the checklist cases that already bump `practice.updatedAt`) all rebuild `state.data` without updating the `data.version` and `data.lastSync` fields. Callers that rely on `lastSync` for sync logic or on `version` for migration compatibility (see `loadData` in storage.ts, which rejects on version mismatch) will see outdated metadata. Consider centralizing updates so mutations also set `lastSync` to the current timestamp (and bump `version` when the schema changes).

**MERGE_DATA deduplicates by ID only, so remote updates to existing records are silently discarded.** When an incoming team/practice has the same `id` as one already in state, it is filtered out regardless of whether it is newer, so changes made on other devices/clients never get applied and data integrity can be lost. Compare timestamps (e.g. `updatedAt`) for existing IDs and take the newest version, or conflict-resolve explicitly.

**A load error permanently disables persistence.** Once `state.error` is set to `'Failed to load data'`, the `saveData()` guard returns early on every subsequent change, and there is no code path that ever clears that error (only `SAVE_ERROR_MESSAGE` is cleared). As a result, after a transient load failure the user's later edits are never written to storage until the app is restarted with a successful load. Consider clearing/retrying load or using a dedicated `loadFailed` flag scoped to the load lifecycle rather than the shared `error` field.

console.error('Error loading data:', error)
        dispatch({ type: 'SET_ERROR', payload: 'Failed to load data' })

findings.content: Nested ternary chain is not allowed per the review guidelines. The logic here (convert 24h->12h) is correct but hard to read; refactor to a single if/else chain for clarity and to comply with the no-nested-ternary rule.

In JavaScript `total % 12` can be negative when `total` is negative, so `newMonth` can become 0 (or a negative month) instead of a value in 1-12 when shifting a sufficient number of months back (e.g. navigating before year 0, say shiftMonth(0, 1, -13) → total = -13 → newMonth = -1 % 12 + 1 = 0). For positive years/deltas this is harmless, but the non-normalized modulo will produce an invalid month at the boundary. Normalize with ((total % 12) + 12) % 12 to be safe.

The auto-dismiss `setTimeout` is never cleaned up. If the component unmounts before the 5s timer fires, `dismissError`/`setError` is called after unmount (React state-update-on-unmounted warning). Also, successive `handleError` calls within 5s each spawn an orphaned timer. Use `useRef` to track the timer and clear it in a `useEffect` cleanup (and before scheduling a new one), or use `useRef`-guarded `setError`.

`Haptics.notificationAsync` returns a Promise, so a rejection cannot be caught by the synchronous `try/catch`. This leads to unhandled promise rejections when haptics fail. Handle it asynchronously, e.g. `Haptics.notificationAsync(HAPTIC_FEEDBACK[severity]).catch(...)` or make the function `async` and await it inside the try/catch.

`handleError`, `clearError`, `dismissError` are recreated on every render and the function closures (e.g. the one captured by the `setTimeout` in `handleError`) are unstable. Wrap them in `useCallback` (and memoize the returned object with `useMemo`) to keep identities stable and avoid unnecessary re-renders/effect re-runs in consumers.

When `options.teamId` is provided, teams are filtered to just that team regardless of whether any filtered practice actually references it. This can produce an export that contains a team with zero practices (or omits teams that do have practices when no teamId is given but the practice references them — that part is handled, but the teamId branch is inconsistent). It's more consistent to always scope teams to `referencedTeamIds` (optionally intersected with `options.teamId`) so the exported teams always correspond to the exported practices.

const teams = options.teamId
    ? data.data.teams.filter(team => team.id === options.teamId)
    : data.data.teams.filter(team => referencedTeamIds.has(team.id))

findings.content: Practices are filtered by comparing `practice.date` (and the filter boundary) as raw strings with `>=` / `<=`. This only produces correct results when every date is in a consistent, lexicographically comparable format such as ISO 8601 (`YYYY-MM-DD`). Any variation (e.g. `MM/DD/YYYY` or timestamps with time zones) silently yields incorrect filter results. Prefer parsing to comparable values (e.g. `new Date(...)` or `Date.parse`) before comparing, or at least normalize the format first.

      return (!start || time >= Date.parse(start)) && (!end || time <= Date.parse(end))

findings.content: The search filter calls `.toLowerCase()` on `practice.location`, `practice.name` and `(practice.headCoach ?? practice.coach)` without any null guard. Although the zod `PracticeSchema` declares these as required, the data is loaded from storage via `JSON.parse(...) as HeatSafetyData` with no runtime validation, so malformed/legacy stored data could contain null/undefined for these fields and make the filter throw. Defensively guard the field access (e.g. `(practice.location ?? '').toLowerCase()`) to keep this pure function safe.

findings.content: Unhandled promise rejection: `impactAsync`, `notificationAsync`, and `selectionAsync` are async functions (they return Promises). The try/catch only catches synchronous errors (e.g. require/reference errors), but if the haptic call itself rejects asynchronously, the rejection is not caught and will surface as an unhandled promise rejection warning/crash. Attach `.catch()` to handle rejection gracefully, e.g. `void haptics.impactAsync(...).catch(() => console.log('Haptic feedback not available'));`. The same problem exists in `triggerNotification` and `selection`.
findings.suggestion_code: haptics.impactAsync(haptics.ImpactFeedbackStyle[style]).catch(() => console.log('Haptic feedback not available'));

findings.content: This same switch statement mapping `hapticType` to `HapticFeedback` methods is duplicated four times (in `HapticButton`, `HapticIconButton`, `HapticTouchable`, and `useHapticFeedback`). This violates DRY and increases maintenance risk — adding a new haptic type requires touching every copy. Extract a helper, e.g. `triggerHaptic(type)` that performs the switch, and call it from each component/hook.

`HapticProvider` is a no-op: it only renders `children` and fully ignores both its `enabled` and `defaultType` props. This provides no global haptic control and may mislead consumers into believing their configuration is being applied. Either implement a context backed by `enabled`/`defaultType` (and have the hooks/components consume it), or remove this component/document that it is currently a placeholder.

The implementation only applies the base Rothfusz regression polynomial without the two official NWS corrective adjustments: (1) when RH < 13% and temperature is 80–112°F, an adjustment of `ADJUSTMENT = [(13 - RH) / 4] * sqrt[(17 - |T - 95|) / 17]` must be subtracted; (2) when RH > 85% and temperature is 80–87°F, `ADJUSTMENT = [(RH - 85) / 10] * [(87 - T) / 5]` must be added. Since the validation bounds allow RH down to 0% and the NWS formula is only calibrated to these conditions, omitting these corrections produces inaccurate (overstated/understated) heat index values in the dry or hot-humid ranges. Consider applying these correction terms for precision.

NaN inputs are not rejected by the validation: all four comparison checks use `<`/`>` which are `false` when the value is `NaN`. As a result `calculateHeatIndex(NaN, 50)` passes validation and the formula propagates NaN to the return via `Math.max(NaN, T)`. Consider guarding with `Number.isFinite()` so non-finite (NaN / Infinity) inputs throw instead of silently producing NaN results.

The memoization cache evicts the first-inserted (FIFO) key whenever the cache exceeds 1000 entries. In a weather/athlete-monitoring use case, common temperature/humidity pairs are likely to be hit repeatedly, so a FIFO eviction policy can repeatedly evict frequently-used entries, reducing cache hit rate. A simple LRU (refresh key order on access) approach would preserve hot entries more effectively even with the size cap.

Orphaned checklists are silently dropped: if a top-level `checklists` entry does not match any practice id (or the practice lookup fails), it is discarded with no warning and never surfaces in the import result. Additionally, `[...existing, ...mine]` only performs concatenation with no deduplication, so if the same checklist already exists in `practice.checklists` AND appears in the top-level `checklists`, it will be imported twice. Consider deduplicating by checklist id and, at minimum, collecting/logging unmatched checklists instead of dropping them.

Type-safety of id matching: `practiceId` and `practice.id` are compared with `===` after only `Array.isArray` type narrowing (which does not validate the shape of checklist entries). A missing/malformed `practiceId` or `id` will silently mismatch and drop otherwise valid checklist data. Consider runtime-validating the id fields (e.g., requiring a non-empty string) before matching, and skip entries that fail validation so the mismatch is visible.

The generic catch swallows the original validation error, which makes diagnosing real import failures (e.g., exactly which field is malformed) very difficult for maintainers/users. Preserve the underlying error — for example `catch (err) { throw new Error('Import data does not match the expected format', { cause: err }) }` (or include `err.message` in the message) — while keeping the user-facing message friendly.

In merge mode the imported `version` and `lastSync` metadata are discarded in favor of the existing dataset's values. If the imported payload carries newer sync metadata (e.g., a more recent `lastSync` or a bumped schema `version`), this can leave the merged dataset stale or with an outdated schema version after a successful import. Decide which metadata should win (imported vs existing) and apply it deterministically rather than always keeping `existing` values.

`Math.abs(diffTime)` treats future dates the same as past dates, so an upcoming practice (e.g. tomorrow) is labeled 'Yesterday' and next week is labeled '7 days ago'. Since this utility is used for practice dates, handle the sign of the difference and return future labels (e.g. 'Tomorrow', 'In X days') when `date > now`.

The 'short' format is month/day only (e.g. '9/7') with no year, so practices from different years on the same month/day collide into a single group. Include the year in the date key (while still using the short label for display) so each group is unique per year.

The calendar map uses `practice.date` directly as the key, while the generated dates use `date.toISOString().split('T')[0]` (UTC yyyy-mm-dd). If `practice.date` is not in exactly that UTC date-only format (e.g. it includes a time component or a localized format), lookups like `practiceMap[dateKey]` will always miss and `hasPractices`/`practiceCount` will be zero. Normalize both keys to the same format before comparison.

findings.content: `createMobileTeamSections` iterates over the passed teams array to build sections, so passing `[]` yields zero team sections — the comment claiming 'will use all teams' is not backed by the implementation. Pass the actual teams (or change `createMobileTeamSections` to accept an optional teams argument that defaults to all teams from practices).

`toISOString()` returns the UTC date, so in time zones ahead of UTC a local 'today' can compare against yesterday's UTC date (and vice-versa), causing off-by-one in `isToday`/`isTomorrow`. Build the 'today' reference using local date components (e.g. year/month/day of `new Date()`) instead of the UTC timestamp.

The heuristic `backgroundColor.startsWith('#f')` misclassifies many dark colors as light. For example `#f00000` (dark red) or `#f50a0a` start with '#f' but are dark, so this returns `PRIMARY` (near-black text) on a dark background — producing unreadable low-contrast text. This directly contradicts the file's stated goal of high-contrast outdoor visibility. Prefer a proper luminance/contrast-ratio calculation (e.g. reuse the `isLightColor` logic) instead of prefix heuristics.

`isLightColor` assumes a 6-digit hex string and has no input validation. For 3-digit hex (`#fff`), `rgb()` strings, `rgba()` strings, or any malformed input, `parseInt` returns `NaN`, and the luminance computed from `NaN` is `NaN`, causing the `luminance > 0.5` comparison to silently return `false` (dark) for every invalid input. Add a guard that validates the format and returns a sane default, and use `slice` instead of the deprecated `substr`.

`String.prototype.substr` is deprecated. Prefer `slice`/`substring`. Additionally, the hex-to-RGB parsing block here is duplicated verbatim from `isLightColor`; consider extracting a small shared helper (`hexToRgb`) to avoid divergence and reduce duplication.

The `page` and `setPage` state are created and returned but never referenced internally — `handleLoadMore` calls `onLoadMore()` without incrementing `page`, and nothing else uses `page`. This is effectively dead state and signals incomplete pagination logic. Either wire `page` into `onLoadMore` (and clear/reset on data change) or remove it to avoid confusion.

The timer created in `setTimeout` is never cleared on unmount. If the component unmounts while throttled, the callback can still fire (setting `inThrottle.current` on an unmounted ref) and the timeout holds the callback/closure unnecessarily — a memory leak. Clear the timeout on unmount via `useEffect` cleanup.

`new Image()` is a DOM/browser-only API and does not exist in React Native's runtime. Calling `preloadImages` in a RN app will throw a ReferenceError. Use a RN-compatible approach such as `Image.prefetch(uri)` from `react-native`, or guard for environment.

`global.performance.memory` is a Chromium-only (web) API and is not available in React Native; this branch will silently never execute on RN, so `memoryUsage` stays `null`. Additionally, `total` could be 0 (or `used` from an incompatible object) causing `used / total` = `NaN`. Use a RN device-memory API or guard with an env check and floor `total` to avoid division by zero.

Using `JSON.stringify` on every item for the key is expensive for large lists and produces unstable identity — any field change regenerates the key, breaking item identity across re-renders and causing incorrect reuse of cells. Prefer a stable unique id field on the item; only fall back to index when the data type guarantees it.

`getItemLayout` hard-codes every row at 80px height. If any item has a different height, `FlatList` will miscalculate scroll offsets and `onEndReached` firing, and `DataDetectorType`/cell measurement will be wrong. Only provide `getItemLayout` when the height is truly uniform; otherwise drop it and let the list measure dynamically.

End date inclusivity bug: `new Date(endDate)` when `endDate` is a date-only string (e.g. '2026-09-07') resolves to midnight at the start of that day. Any practice on the end date occurring after 00:00 will be excluded from the result. To make the range inclusive for the whole end day, end at 23:59:59.999 of endDate or set `end.setHours(23, 59, 59, 999)` when no time component is provided.

const start = new Date(startDate);
  const end = new Date(endDate);

findings.content: When the team has practices but none of them have checklists, `teamPractices.flatMap(...)` yields an empty array and `Math.max(...[])` returns `-Infinity`, which is a misleading return value (callers may render it). Guard against an empty heat-index array (similar to the empty-practices check).

NaN bug: the guard only checks `teamPractices.length === 0`, but if the team has practices with zero checklists, `allHeatIndices` is empty and `sum / allHeatIndices.length` computes `0 / 0 === NaN`. Check `allHeatIndices.length === 0` instead (or in addition) before dividing.

findings.content: `Math.max(...array)` with a large heat-index array risks hitting the call-stack argument limit (RangeError). Consider a reduce-based fold for robustness: `arr.reduce((max, v) => Math.max(max, v), ...)`. Same pattern is used in getPracticeRiskLevel/getPracticeRiskColor/getPracticeStats.

Lexicographic `.sort()` on time strings only yields correct chronological order if times are zero-padded ('HH:mm'). For unpadded values such as '9:00' vs '10:00', '10:00' sorts before '9:00', making earliest/latest times wrong. Convert to comparable values (e.g. minutes since midnight) before sorting, or parse the times numerically.

`getCurrentWeekPractices` assumes the week starts on Sunday via `now.getDay()`. In locales where Monday is the start of the week (ISO 8601), this yields an unexpected Monday boundary and can misclassify Sunday practices. Consider a configurable/locale-aware week start.
`new Date(practice.date)` is parsed twice inside the filter chain. Minor performance nit, but it can be flattened/hoisted to avoid redundant parsing across potentially large practice lists.

findings.content: Invalid date handling in sort: if `practice.date` is null/undefined or not a valid date string, `new Date(...).getTime()` returns `NaN`. The comparator `NaN - NaN` yields `NaN`, which the sort algorithm treats as 0 in some engines but leads to unstable/incorrect ordering. Add a guard that treats invalid dates as oldest (e.g. coerce `isNaN(time) ? 0 : time`) so the ordering is deterministic.

Only the `version` field is validated after JSON parsing. A stored value that matches `DATA_VERSION` but is malformed (e.g. missing `data`, `data.teams`, or `data.practices`, or has wrong types) will pass the check and cause runtime errors downstream (e.g. `data.data.teams` throwing when accessed in `getTeams`). Add schema validation of the nested shapes (Array.isArray on teams/practices, typeof checks) before returning parsed data.

`getTeams`/`getPractices` have no try/catch of their own and delegate entirely to `loadData`. Currently safe only because `loadData` swallows all errors and returns defaults, but a future change to `loadData` (e.g. throwing on invalid data) would propagate an uncaught rejection to callers. Wrap these in try/catch and return a safe default (e.g. empty array) to keep the read-only utilities robust.

`getTeams` and `getPractices` each call `loadData()` independently; when several of these are used to render one screen they each re-read and re-parse the full AsyncStorage payload. Consider adding a small read-through cache or a single combined loader to avoid redundant storage I/O when fetching teams and practices together.

Team ID is derived solely from a millisecond timestamp. Multiple calls within the same millisecond (e.g., creating several teams in one tick, or rapid create/delete in the same rendering cycle) yield identical IDs, which can corrupt data integrity when IDs are used as keys or in lookups. Consider appending a monotonic counter, a random suffix, or using `crypto.randomUUID()` to guarantee uniqueness.

The exclusion `existing.trim().toLowerCase() !== currentTrimmed` skips *every* entry whose lowercased value equals the current name, not just the team being edited. If another distinct team owns a same-name-different-case entry (e.g. editing "team a" while an existing separate team is "TEAM A"), that entry is silently ignored and the name is falsely reported as available. The check should only exclude the specific team being edited (e.g., by comparing team IDs), not by name equality.

Error messages at the same path overwrite each other. If a single field produces multiple validation issues (e.g., a value that violates both min and max, or a nested object with multiple sub-errors), only the last message is retained and earlier ones are silently lost. Consider aggregating messages instead, e.g. appending with a separator or collecting the first issue per path, so no diagnostic information is dropped.

ChecklistSchema requires `deviceInfo` and `timestamp` (both plain required strings), but ChecklistFormSchema omits both fields and makes them absent. If a ChecklistFormSchema-validated payload is passed directly to validateChecklist(), parsing will fail at runtime because these required fields are missing. Either include these fields in the form schema (with defaults) or make them optional in ChecklistSchema, otherwise the two schemas are inconsistent for the same domain entity.

This is a redundant duplication: `ChecklistEntry` is identical to `Checklist`, which is already exported above (`export type Checklist = z.infer<typeof ChecklistSchema>`). Having two names for the same type confuses consumers. Remove one of the duplicates (the comment says it exists for 'new models', but it simply re-exports the same type).

`teamId` is validated only as an arbitrary non-empty string with no format or existence check, while all other ID fields (checklist.id, practiceId, etc.) enforce a strict pattern (`/^[a-zA-Z][a-zA-Z0-9-]*$/`). A malformed or typo'd teamId reference could silently pass validation and produce orphaned practices. Align it with the same ID pattern used elsewhere for consistency and integrity.
findings.suggestion_code: teamId: z.string().regex(/^[a-zA-Z][a-zA-Z0-9-]*$/, 'Team ID must start with a letter and can contain letters, numbers, and hyphens'),

findings.content: This custom safeParse reimplements behavior that Zod already provides natively via `schema.safeParse()`, which returns a discriminated `{ success, data } | { success, error }` result without throwing. The custom version also manually converts errors via getValidationErrors (which has the message-overwrite issue noted above). Prefer using Zod's built-in safeParse for consistency, less code, and to avoid version drift (e.g. reliance on `error.errors` vs `error.issues` across Zod major versions).

Content paths only scan `./src/**` and `./tests/**`. For a web build (e.g., Vite), the root `index.html`/template entry files are usually outside `src` and would be missed, causing utility classes used there to be purged/missing in production. Confirm whether any HTML/template files live outside `src`; if so add them (e.g., `"./*.html"`). If this is a pure React Native/NativeWind project, these paths are fine.

`Inter_400Regular`, `Inter_500Medium`, etc. are Expo/expo-font loading aliases, not standard CSS font family names. In a web/browser runtime these will not resolve to any available font and the client will silently fall back to `system-ui`/`Arial`, breaking the intended design. Ensure the fonts are actually loaded under these exact family names at runtime (e.g., via `expo-font` on native, or `@font-face` with the same family name for web).

Minor type signature drift: the declaration marks the label parameter as optional (`label?: string`), while the implementation in tests/setup.ts declares it as a required positional parameter `toHaveAccessibilityLabel(received, label: string)`. The optionality could mask a test that forgets to pass a label (though the implementation does tolerate undefined internally). For consistency, either make the declaration required, or reflect that undefined means "check the prop exists" explicitly in the type.
findings.suggestion_code: toHaveAccessibilityLabel(label: string): R;

findings.content: The mock factory spreads `require('react-reanimated')`, but the installed package (and the module being mocked) is `react-native-reanimated`. The package name `react-reanimated` does not exist, so this require will throw when the factory runs, breaking every test that imports reanimated. Use `require('react-native-reanimated')` for the spread (though note that spreading the real native module inside the mock is also fragile — prefer fully overriding just the needed hooks).

findings.content: Silencing console.error globally in `beforeAll` hides all error output from tests. Real failures (React render errors, native module warnings, rejected promises that surface via console.error) will be silently swallowed, making debugging difficult and masking genuinely broken tests. Prefer scoping the suppression to specific tests (e.g. within `spyOn(...).mockImplementation` + `mockRestore` in only the tests that need it) rather than disabling it app-wide for the entire suite.

`useRoute` always returns `{ params: {} }` regardless of the actual navigation params the component would receive. A component reading `route.params.id` etc. will silently get `undefined`, so tests can pass against the wrong assumptions about navigation state. Consider allowing per-test override of the returned params (e.g. via a mutable mock or a helper) so real route params can be exercised.

The document picker mock always resolves with `{ assets: [] }` (no files). Any test branch that expects a picked file will instead hit the empty-list/error path of the component under test, giving false positives/negatives about picker behavior. Consider exposing a configurable return value so tests can simulate a successful pick.

`lib` only includes `es6`, but `target` is `es2020`. Since `lib` is explicitly overridden here (over any base config), standard library definitions for newer ES features (e.g. `es2017`+ like `Object.entries`, `es2018.AsyncIterable`, `es2020` such as `BigInt`/`Promise.allSettled`/global `this`) will be missing, potentially causing type errors when those APIs are used in src/tests. Align `lib` with `target` by adding the newer ES lib entries (e.g. `es2020`) instead of only `es6`.

The broad `@/*` alias already resolves any path under `./src/*`, so the more specific mappings (`@/components/*`, `@/utils/*`, `@/context/*`, `@/hooks/*`, `@/types/*`, `@/tests/*`) are redundant and rely on less-specific mapping precedence. Keeping both broad and narrow mappings can cause ambiguity/confusion about which one applies and makes the config harder to maintain. Consider removing the redundant sub-path aliases and relying solely on `@/*`, or making them consistent with the actual feature structure.
